Neonatal pygmy right whales (Caperea marginata) enter the world at a relatively modest size compared to other mysticetes, with total length at birth measuring approximately 180 centimeters [Lb = approximately 180 centimeters], a dimension that places them among the smaller cetacean neonates. Field records and stranding data indicate that newborns typically range between 1.6 and 2.2 meters in body length, a span that reflects the species’ overall diminutive adult proportions. The wet weight at birth for a calf is estimated at roughly 76.5 kilograms [Wwb = roughly 76.5 kilograms], a value derived from allometric scaling relationships with maternal mass and consistent with the low absolute birth mass predicted for a baleen whale of this size. This relatively low neonatal mass likely imposes a high degree of parental investment, as the calf must undergo substantial somatic growth before achieving nutritional independence. The suckling period is prolonged, reflecting the slow life-history pace typical of small-bodied cetaceans that occupy cold, productive waters in the Southern Hemisphere. Observations of mother-calf pairs suggest a close spatial association during the first several months postpartum.

A significant developmental milestone for the pygmy right whale is the transition to nutritional independence, which is marked by weaning. The total length at weaning has been recorded at approximately 325 centimeters , a body size that typically corresponds with an age of about one year after birth. Under the core body temperature conditions characteristic of this endothermic mammal, which are maintained near 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the time since birth at weaning is estimated at 365 days [tx = 365 days]. This weaning timeline, equivalent to a full annual cycle, suggests that calves exploit a single productive season to accumulate sufficient energy reserves before the maternal-offspring bond is severed. Following weaning, the juvenile enters a protracted period of independent growth, during which it must refine its foraging skills on krill and other small crustaceans. The slow rate of postnatal development relative to other cetaceans underscores the conservative energetic strategy employed by this species, which occupies a narrow trophic niche in the Southern Ocean gyre systems.

Sexual maturation in the pygmy right whale occurs after a lengthy juvenile phase, a pattern consistent with the species’ inferred low metabolic turnover and delayed life-history schedule. Under the stable core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] typical of all cetaceans, females attain puberty at a time since birth of approximately 10 years [tp = approximately 10 years]. At this developmental threshold, the total length at puberty commonly falls within a range of 5 to 6 meters [Lp = 5 to 6 meters], with a central estimate around 550 centimeters [Lp = around 550 centimeters]. This substantial body size relative to adult dimensions indicates that females must accumulate considerable somatic tissue before the onset of ovarian cycling and reproductive competence. The delay in reaching sexual maturity, which is comparable to that observed in the gray whale Eschrichtius robustus, reflects the energetic demands of growing to a size that can support the caloric load of gestation and subsequent lactation. Puberty is not followed immediately by successful breeding; first parturition often occurs several years later, as females require further experience and condition to carry a pregnancy to term.

Female pygmy right whales reach their ultimate body size following the completion of somatic growth, an event that typically coincides with or follows the first successful reproductive event. The ultimate total length for females has been measured at 625 centimeters [Li = 625 centimeters], with most asymptotic reports falling between 6 and 6.5 meters. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 3,200,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 3,200,000 grams], or roughly 3.2 metric tons, placing them among the smallest adult baleen whales by mass. This modest adult mass is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes slow, sustained growth over rapid attainment of large body size, a trade-off likely shaped by the relatively low productivity of their subantarctic foraging grounds. The reproductive output of this species is thought to be correspondingly low. Analogy with the gray whale suggests that the maximum reproduction rate, sustained at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], equates to approximately 0.0014 calves per day [Ri = approximately 0.0014 calves per day], a figure that in natural language corresponds to one calf every two years [Ri = one calf every two years], with each pregnancy yielding one calf per litter [N_R_i = one calf per litter].

Gestation in the pygmy right whale is a prolonged process, as is typical for mysticetes that undertake seasonal migrations or inhabit cold waters with predictable prey blooms. The gestation time has been estimated at 320 days [tg = 320 days], a duration that spans approximately 10.5 months when measured under the species’ stable core thermoregulatory regime of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This length of pregnancy is consistent with that of other balaenid and eschrichtiid whales of comparable body size, reflecting the extended period required for foetal development in a large, precocial mammal that gives birth to a single, well-developed calf. The slow foetal growth rate, inferred from the gestation time and neonatal length, suggests a conservative intrauterine energetic investment that aligns with the overall low metabolic pace of the species. Following parturition, the female faces a substantial energetic cost from lactation, which likely imposes a multi-year interbirth interval. The lifespan of the pygmy right whale, based on comparative data from the gray whale sustained at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], is estimated at 70 years [am = 70 years], a longevity that permits only a limited number of reproductive events over a lifetime, given the protracted intervals between successive calves. This combination of delayed maturity, extended gestation, slow weaning, and long lifespan places Caperea marginata at the extreme slow end of the life-history continuum among baleen whales, a strategy that makes the species particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic perturbations such as bycatch or prey depletion.
